name: Marguerite Yellow
lede: Marguerite Yellow is a pale, buttery yellow first plated by Ridgway in 1912, and so close to a color Wikipedia lists as Lemon Meringue that the two amount to the same paint.

sections.title: A 1912 plate, a modern duplicate
sections.body:
Ridgway's atlas places this value at plate XXX, hue 23′′, tone f, first recorded in 1912 [1]. Maerz and Paul's own 1930 dictionary independently lands on the same plate position and the same year, 10 C 3, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 classifies it as a pale yellow green [1][2]. The flower marguerite, a kind of daisy, gives the name, though neither book explains why this particular pale shade was chosen for it rather than a brighter one [1].

Our library's own color match finds a near-duplicate, Lemon Meringue, within about 2 units, close enough that the two likely read as identical on any screen [3]. Its listed neighbor is [[lemon-meringue|Seafoam Green]], an unrelated cool color that happens to sit nearby in lightness and saturation rather than in hue [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Marguerite Yellow covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 441 works, about one in fifty, as photographed [4]. It is most over-represented in paintings from Iran, China and Switzerland, and John Singer Sargent carries it in 14 of his 287 archived paintings [4]. The painter most strongly tied to it, relative to his output, is Pieter Gerardus van Os, at over sixteen times the expected rate [4]. These remain photographs of aged, varnished canvases read as screen colors, not pigment tests [4].
